newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy opposition leads in big cities, League loses.
newsitem.headline: Italy opposition leads in big cities, League loses.

text.p: Italy's main opposition alliance led in mayoral races in the key cities of Milan and Turin after a first round of voting on Sunday ended the separatist Northern League's control of the country's business capital.

Milan's outgoing mayor Marco Formentini, elected in 1993 at the height of the League's popularity, trailed a poor third to opponents from the centre-right Freedom Alliance and the governing centre-left Olive Tree bloc, exit polls showed.

Industrialist Gabriele Albertini of the Freedom Alliance led in Milan with 39 to 43 percent of the vote against 25 to 29 for his Olive Tree rival Aldo Fumagalli, the forecasts said. The two men will contest a second round run-off on May 11.

The Freedom Alliance also led in Turin, Italy's northern industrial heart, where challenger Raffaele Costa was forecast to win 39 to 43 percent of the vote against 35 to 39 for outgoing centre-left mayor Valentino Castellani.

Milan was the biggest prize in elections for mayors and local councils in more than 1,100 towns and cities in the first big test of electoral support since Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition won last April's general election.

In four other big cities at stake, the Olive Tree was ahead in the northeast port of Trieste, Ancona on the Adriatic coast and Reggio Calabria on the toe of Italy, while the Freedom Alliance candidate led in Catanzaro in the south.

Olive Tree politicians said it was too early to interpret the elections but the opposition, which had billed the vote as an opportunity for people to oppose Prodi, said the forecasts pointed to a slap in the face for the government.
"The results in the mayoral races...show that the Olive Tree is suffering a real debacle," said Rocco Buttiglione, leader of the centrist CDU party in the Freedom Alliance bloc.

The exit polls, conducted by Abacus for broadcasters RAI and Fininvest, forecast that Formentini would win only 17 to 21 percent of the vote in Milan in a further sign of waning support for the Northern League's separatist agenda.
League leader Umberto Bossi brushed off Formentini's defeat and a poor showing in Turin, saying southern Italian "immigrants" in the cities would never vote for his party.

He said he would advise supporters to "go the mountains" for the second round and not vote of anyone. "The north has to prepare for the independence struggle to come and not give even half a vote to the parties from Rome," he said.
About 9.4 million people, one fifth of the national electorate, were eligible to vote in the elctions. Vote-counting was to begin on Monday morning with official results later in the day.

The Prodi government's popularity has suffered through resentment at tax increases imposed to cut the budget deficit and try to squeeze Italy into the first wave of countries to join Europe's planned single currency.

It had sought to divorce the municipal polls from its own performance, clouded by a battle of wills between centrists in the coalition and the hard-left Communist Refoundation party which provides Prodi with his parliamentary majority.

The Communist Refoundation's shadow appeared to weigh over the mayoral battles, with the party running alone in the main contests and suggesting it could seek a high price for swinging its voters behind centre-left candidates in the second round.
Party leader Fausto Bertinotti, preparing to do battle with Prodi over planned reforms to the welfare state, said the exit polls showed the Olive Tree could not win without his backing.

"In Turin and Milan the Olive Tree is trailing the Freedom Alliance simply because it did not ally with Communist Refoundation. Otherwise we would have won," Bertinotti said. "I hope the Olive Tree does not make a suicidal choice."
